affected.versions: >= 2.0.0, <= 6.5.6 (the record gives introduced 2.0.0 and last known affected version range <= 6.5.6)

reading.notes: The advisory's sentence names only 6.5.6, but the same record gives a range: S1 also has the line "introduced": "2.0.0", so the versions listed as affected run from 2.0.0 up to and including 6.5.6. The excerpts show code for 6.5.6 and 6.5.7 only, so the start at 2.0.0 rests on the record alone. The missing check is about the top bit of the first byte of r and of s, not about r or s being the number zero. The difference shown is only in the function that reads DER-encoded signatures (_importDER): 6.5.7 adds the line if ((data[p.place] & 128) !== 0) { followed by return false, once for r and once for s; 6.5.6 has neither, and the "Leading zeroes" check is the same in both. What the sources show is 6.5.6 accepting a second byte form of the same r and s (the number written without a zero byte in front, so that its first byte has the top bit set); they do not show a signature being accepted for a message it was not made for.
reading.weakness: When it reads an ECDSA signature in DER form, the affected code does not check that the top bit of the first byte is zero for each of the signature's two numbers, r and s. As a result it accepts signature bytes that the fixed version refuses, so the same signature is accepted in more than one byte form (the advisory calls this signature malleability).

reading.notes: The signature wrongly accepted here is one whose bytes are not written in the strict format; the sources do not say that a signature is accepted for a message that was never signed. The advisory's sentence names only version 6.5.6, but the record's range starts earlier, on a separate S1 line: "introduced": "5.2.1". In the code excerpts the one difference is that getLength in 6.5.7 (S2) returns false when a length spread over extra bytes starts with a 0x00 byte; 6.5.6 (S3) has no such check and reads a length padded with a leading zero byte whenever its value is above 0x7f. The excerpts show only this one function, so any other changes in 6.5.7 are not shown here.
reading.weakness: When it reads an ECDSA signature, the affected elliptic accepts signatures written in the looser BER format, not only the strict DER format. As a result the same signature can be rewritten as different bytes and still be accepted, which the advisory calls signature malleability.

test.reason: No test yet: By the lab's reading of the code excerpts, the affected version wrongly reads a length only when it is padded with a leading zero byte and its value is above 0x7f (128 or more); the seven BER cases are rewrites of a P-256 signature whose lengths are 69, 32 and 33, so the three padded ones (9, 68, 115) stay below that line and the other four have no padded length. Showing this weakness needs a longer signature from a larger curve, and the building block cannot run another curve or a new case.

affected.versions: 4.0.0 (introduced) up to and including 6.5.6 (last known affected version range: <= 6.5.6)

reading.notes: The advisory's sentence names only 6.5.6, but the same record's version data has the line "introduced": "4.0.0", so do not read it as 6.5.6 alone. The sources describe changing an existing EdDSA signature by removing or appending zero-valued bytes; they do not describe making a signature for a message that was never signed, and they do not mention ECDSA. The code excerpts match the record: 6.5.7 adds one line that 6.5.6 lacks, which requires a signature given as an array of bytes to be exactly twice the encoding length and otherwise fails an assertion with the message 'Signature has invalid size'. The excerpts show only this constructor, not how a caller reports that failure.
reading.weakness: When elliptic reads an EdDSA signature, it does not check that the signature has the expected length. So a signature with zero-valued bytes removed or appended is not refused for its length, and the same signature can be presented in more than one byte form (the advisory calls this signature malleability).

weakness_quote.text: In the Elliptic package 6.5.6 for Node.js, EDDSA signature malleability occurs because there is a missing signature length check, and thus zero-valued bytes can be removed or appended.

None of its 484 cases is an EdDSA signature, so none reaches the part of the library that has the weakness; the ECDSA cases with zero bytes added or removed go through a different signature reader and would be testing something else.
